extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, counsel and parties in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing requests for reconsideration of USPTO Director decisions in Office disciplinary proceedings, and the disciplinary rules cited (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23, 10.77, 10.18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single request for reconsideration or modification of a final decision by the USPTO Director may be filed within twenty days from the date of entry of the decision, but no request shall be granted unless it is based on newly discovered evidence or error of law or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requestor must demonstrate that any newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered any earlier by due diligence; § 11.56(c) is similar to Fed.R.Civ.P. 59(e) and 60; requests that merely rehash previously presented arguments or express disagreement are improper; reconsideration is an 'extraordinary remedy' and should be used sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness requirement for reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for reconsideration or modification must be filed within twenty days from the date of entry of the USPTO Director's decision (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not filed within the 20-day window, the request is untimely and cannot be considered under § 11.56(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly discovered evidence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify reconsideration, evidence relied upon must be 'newly discovered' and the requestor must show the evidence could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials that were publicly available prior to the hearing (e.g., USPTO rules or publicly posted documents) are not 'new evidence' because they could have been obtained and relied upon earlier; mere references to previously available documents do not meet this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on rehashing prior arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for reconsideration is not a vehicle to state disagreement with a final judgment or to reargue matters previously presented to the tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere disagreement or repetition of previously-made arguments is an improper basis for reconsideration (cases cited: Hutchinson v. Staton; Above the Belt, Inc. v. Mel Bohannan Roofing, Inc.). Reconsideration is appropriate only in limited circumstances such as mistaken apprehension, misunderstanding, or decision outside issues presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration is an extraordinary, rarely granted remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration motions are to be used sparingly and relief is limited to extraordinary circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions analogized (e.g., Rule 60(b)(6) limited to 'extraordinary circumstances'); institutional practice disfavors routine reconsideration—examples of appropriate grounds include patently misunderstood party, decision outside adversarial issues, or error of apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — proscription of disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10.23(a) proscribes engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director concluded a plain reading of § 10.23(a) shows there is no element of intent required by that provision; claims that all provisions of the Rules of Professional Conduct require intent are unsupported. False certification under disciplinary rules is not the same as inequitable conduct in patent litigation (Therasense inapposite).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15) / § 10.18 — signing papers in violation of certification rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Signing a paper filed with the USPTO in violation of the provisions of 37 C.F.R. § 10.18 (e.g., certifying a reasonable inquiry) is proscribed under § 10.23(c)(15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner's certification that a reasonable inquiry was made may be disciplined if the certification is false; false certification supports disciplinary sanctions under the USPTO rules separate from inequitable-conduct doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10.77(c) proscribes neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office may sanction neglect even if the conduct was inadvertent or an error in judgment; intent is not a prerequisite to a § 10.77(c) violation as previously argued by the respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of federal civil procedure standards as guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (e.g., Rules 59(e), 60) are not binding in USPTO administrative proceedings but can provide useful guidance in judging motions for reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations to federal cases and rules are used for persuasive analogies on standards for reconsideration and extraordinary relief, but administrative rules (37 C.F.R.) control the PTO process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and limits of judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: A party dissatisfied with the Director's decision may seek judicial review on the record in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review must be sought 'within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action'; local court rules (e.g., E.D.Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5) apply.
